tells: 'What these people see that others miss, Imam ʿAli (ʿa) describes' — fronted object that holds back the subject; Author A opens plainly with subject first, e.g. 'Imam ʿAli (ʿa) describes what these people see'

'Sheikh Bahmanpour is careful about the reason. There is nothing wrong, in the shariʿa, with being rich.' — jumps to wealth with no link to the last sentence; Author A picks up the last idea before moving on
'The Qur'an does not describe them as a theory. It describes them as believers.' — a neat not-X-but-Y closing line; Author A ends paragraphs on the plain point, not on a turned phrase
'But they do not think about themselves' — a sentence opening on 'But' in an otherwise choppy run; Author A uses 'Yet' or joins the clauses with a semicolon

'Surah Fatir adds: "Only those of Allah's servants having knowledge fear Him"' — claim, colon and bare quotation stacked together; Author A builds the quotation into the sentence ('Surah Fatir says that only those...')
'Tawhid is simple to say and very hard to grasp' — a slogan-like antithesis with the intensifier 'very'; Author A would write it without the flourish ('requires a great deal of')
'with a fear that is not about punishment at all' — emphatic 'at all' is a spoken register; Author A says it once and plainly
'Higher still is a verse about God's oneness.' — an inverted, ranking opener; Author A would write 'A verse in Surah Al ʿImran goes further'

Opens by picking up the previous point ('rests on the same humility'), uses plain first-person-plural 'we', and the second paragraph picks up 'God's invitation' from the last sentence before it. The register is measured and plain.
Raises the reader's concern plainly, then 'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads this verse as...' with glosses set in the sentence, and ends on a plain sourced point, the way Author A handles verses.

'Access to these words is where an ordinary believer already stands on the path.' — an abstract, slightly garbled topic sentence; Author A would state the point concretely
'Part One began... Chapter Two showed... This chapter has found' — a recap paragraph summing up the chapter; Author A moves forward rather than summing up

The quotation is introduced in the sentence and then explained ('The line names God as...'). 'Let's take them in turn' matches Author A's 'Let's start', and 'the faculty behind them' echoes Author A's receiver argument in the same plain rhythm.

Opens with a conditional that picks up the last idea ('If the faculty can be repaired...'), as Author A does ('If the signs are present and plain...'). The verse is explained by plain reasoning, and the paragraph hands on to the next verse ('goes further, giving them another name').

'about something else: catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive to them' — two colons stacked in one sentence; Author A keeps to one colon and starts a new sentence ('Islamic mysticism is about catching the signs of Allah: ...')
'and he does not soften it.' — an editorialising closer; Author A ends on the gloss ('the gravest charge in Islam.')
'His closing words to his first class were stronger.' — wordy, with a noun-phrase subject; Author A would write 'He ended his first lecture more strongly.'
'opened his course by pointing out that' — a wordy lead-in; Author A states the point directly ('People take up the inner life for different reasons.')
'Chapter One met the same severance' — chapter number spelled out; Author A writes 'Chapter 1'
'They keep their families, their friends, and their place in society' — serial comma, which Author A never uses (cf. 'families, friends and a place in society')

'The severance the prayers ask for is therefore in the heart, not in the household or the marketplace.' — a tidy 'therefore' summary line at the paragraph's end; Author A does not restate the point to close
'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide.' — a balanced antithesis whose referents ('One', 'the other') are not clear; Author A names each scholar
'Neither makes powers the aim of the path.' — a summary line closing the paragraph; Author A ends on the source's point
'Mutahhari's words show why seeking them would be: the goal has become something other than God' — a claim and colon stacked on an elliptical 'would be'; Author A writes complete, plain clauses
'For him the feats are beside the point: something a student should look past' — an idiomatic restatement of a quotation already given; Author A explains once

The quotations are built into the sentences with reporting verbs ('tells the traveller that he "has no right..."'), as with Author A's Shomali and Khomeini quotations. There is no closing flourish, and the paragraphs follow the scholars in order.

Short, plain declaratives ('People take up the inner life for different reasons.'), a single colon per sentence, and a plain close on the gloss ('the gravest charge in Islam'), with no editorial tail.
